title: Noche de paz
description: Silent Night in Spanish, Franz Gruber's tune with the words "Noche de paz, noche de amor" as a New York hymnal printed them in 1893, for 2 to 4 singers: all three verses, gentle and lilting in 6/8. The soprano sings the tune, the alto mostly a third or sixth below, the tenor fills the chord and the bass holds mostly the roots on "oo". A stretch song: the tune runs from low C up to F, so take the high and low notes gently, or move the key.

credits.words: Spanish words after Joseph Mohr's German (1816), as printed, unsigned, in El Himnario evangélico (New York, 1893); often credited to Federico Fliedner (in 13 of the 18 hymnals from 1990 on that Hymnary.org indexes), though no printing we have seen before 1964 names him

licence.words: public domain: printed, unsigned, in New York in 1893, and the hymnal's preface says its unnamed editors changed some hymns' phrasing ("nos hemos permitido cambiar en algo la fraseología"); often credited to Federico Fliedner (died 1901), in 13 of the 18 hymnals from 1990 on that Hymnary.org indexes, though no printing we have seen before 1964 names him (see source); the German original by Joseph Mohr (died 1848)
licence.tune: public domain: Franz Xaver Gruber (died 1863); printed 1893
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella: the alto and tenor sing the words with the tune, holding their syllable through its slurred notes, and the bass holds mostly the roots on "oo" (B under the G7 before each verse's last chord, so 3 singers keep its third); the 1893 hymnal's four parts are unsigned and were used only to check the chords. Accepted exceptions (singable.py): the tune's own range as printed, its top F on "es-tre-", "buen" and "ter-" a semitone above the beginner soprano range and its low C on each verse's last "paz.", "tor." and "gor." a tone below; on those low C's the alto sings E, a third above the tune, so the duet ends with the chord's third; and the tune's passing B in "To-do", "el" and "qué" meets the alto's held B an octave below for one quaver.
licence.source: El Himnario evangélico, para el uso de todas las iglesias (New York: Sociedad Americana de Tratados [American Tract Society], copyright 1893; no editor named on the title page or in the preface), hymn 48, "¡Noche de paz, noche de amor!", p. 38, the tune headed "Holy Night." with no composer or author named, four parts on two staves, in C in 6/8, written here in C in 6/8 (a dotted crotchet is one beat); every pitch of the tune as printed, and its rhythm except the breaths below, the semiquaver pairs the page beams on one syllable ("do", "rre") sung as slurred notes, and "paz" slurred up to the E as printed; verse 1 as underlaid, and verses 2 and 3 as printed below it, sung to the same notes, their last lines sung twice as verse 1 prints it (verses 2 and 3 print it once; the 1907 Himnario provisional marks the repeat); in verse 2 "cam-po | al", "Gra-cias | y" and "glo-rias | en" take a note each, as the 1907 book's metre (8.7.10.10.7.7, the same for every verse) counts them; breaths written in for beginners, in every verse: the last note of lines 1, 3 and 4 and the slurred E that ends line 5 each a semiquaver shorter than printed, the last note of line 2 ("derredor", "pastor", "resplandor") a dotted quaver instead of a dotted crotchet, and the last note of verses 1 and 2 a semiquaver shorter, to leave half a beat before each new line; Princeton Theological Seminary Library's copy, read from the scan at archive.org/details/elhimevangl93amer/page/n43 (scan page n43); the tune checked against the same music and words in the Himnario provisional ... para congregaciones españoles, ed. James Heartt Van Buren (Philadelphia: John C. Winston, 1907), no. 18, "Navidad", tune "Noche Buena", archive.org/details/himnari00vanb/page/n24; the words also in the words-only Himnos evangélicos (New York: American Tract Society, 1894), no. 48, pp. 23 to 24, archive.org/details/himnosevangelic00bart/page/n28, unsigned there too, like most of that book's hymns, among them nos. 47 and 49 (no. 46 is signed "J. B. Cabrera"); the credit to Federico Fliedner: Hymnary.org (opened 2026-11-12) indexes the text in 52 hymnals, with no Spanish credit before 1952, Fliedner first in Culto Cristiano (1964), no. 23, "Federico Fliedner, 1845-1901 (adapt.)", and in 13 of the 18 hymnals from 1990 on; no printing we have seen before 1964 names him, and the 1893, 1894, 1907 and 1915 books never mention him; the 1871 date ("registrada por Federico Fliedner en el año 1871") is found only as one unsourced sentence in El Debate (26 December 2023) and in Spanish Wikipedia; The Cyber Hymnal's page now credits the same verse 1 to Federico Pagura, born 1923, which the 1893 print rules out
